name: Sepiapterin reductase deficiency
aliases: dopa-responsive dystonia due to sepiapterin reductase deficiency

reference.source: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID) / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis caused by SPR mutations, reducing dopamine and serotonin production while sparing systemic phenylalanine handling
A striking feature is that blood phenylalanine is typically normal, so the condition is missed by newborn phenylketonuria screening and often diagnosed late

It presents as a levodopa-responsive dystonia and parkinsonism, frequently with diurnal fluctuation (worse later in the day), developmental delay, oculogyric crises, and sometimes cognitive and behavioural difficulty
Because both dopamine and serotonin are deficient, treatment usually combines levodopa with a serotonin precursor to address the dual neurotransmitter defect
The CSF hallmark is low homovanillic acid and low 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid with raised sepiapterin and dihydrobiopterin, reflecting the block in BH4 regeneration
Diagnosis rests on CSF neurotransmitter and pterin analysis, enzyme studies, and SPR sequencing; early recognition can transform the motor and developmental outcome
reference.pathophysiology: Sepiapterin reductase catalyses the final step of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis. BH4 is the essential cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so its deficiency impairs synthesis of both dopamine and serotonin. Because alternative pathways can regenerate enough BH4 for hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase, systemic phenylalanine metabolism is preserved and newborn screening is normal, yet central monoamine neurotransmission is deficient. The result is a mixed dopaminergic and serotonergic deficiency causing levodopa-responsive dystonia and parkinsonism with diurnal variation, and accumulation of upstream pterins such as sepiapterin and dihydrobiopterin.
additionalDifferentials: GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency (autosomal dominant Segawa dystonia)
Idiopathic early-onset dystonia or juvenile parkinsonism
additionalInvestigations: Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites showing low homovanillic acid and low 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid
CSF pterin profile with raised sepiapterin and dihydrobiopterin
SPR gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Plasma phenylalanine (characteristically normal) and phenylalanine loading test where used
Fibroblast sepiapterin reductase enzyme activity assay
Documented clinical response to combined levodopa and serotonin-precursor therapy
redFlags: Progressive dystonia and parkinsonism in a child mislabelled as cerebral palsy
Marked diurnal fluctuation with severe evening deterioration limiting function
Recurrent oculogyric crises and developmental regression
Behavioural or mood disturbance suggesting serotonergic deficiency needing treatment adjustment
reference.prognosis: With early combined neurotransmitter-precursor therapy many patients show substantial and sustained improvement in motor and developmental function, whereas delayed treatment may leave residual cognitive and motor deficits. The disorder is treatable rather than curable, and long-term follow-up guides dose adjustment.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal newborn phenylalanine screen excludes a BH4-related disorder
Treating only the dopaminergic deficit and omitting serotonin-precursor therapy
Not performing CSF pterin and neurotransmitter analysis, which is central to the diagnosis
Overlooking the diagnosis in older children presenting with fluctuating dystonia and learning difficulty
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
management: Correct the dual neurotransmitter deficit with levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor and a serotonin precursor such as 5-hydroxytryptophan, the definitive treatment
Consider adjunctive folinic acid and titrate therapy carefully against clinical response and CSF metabolite levels
Provide developmental therapies, physiotherapy, and support for dystonia and oculogyric crises
Monitor for levodopa-related dyskinesia and serotonergic adverse effects, adjusting doses accordingly
Recognise and treat early, since this is a treatable disorder in which prompt therapy can transform motor and developmental outcome
Coordinate multidisciplinary care between metabolic medicine and paediatric neurology
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive SPR-related condition
